title: NGC 1365 (MIRI Image)
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365 in mid-infrared light, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1365, The Great Barred Spiral Galaxy · constellation Fornax · about 56 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Janice Lee (NSF's NOIRLab); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A huge galaxy fills the whole frame, with its spiral arms running off the lower right edge and a bright white, slightly pinkish core shaped like an elongated oval just off center. This is NGC 1365, a double-barred spiral about 56 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax, seen by Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI).

At these wavelengths, clumps of dust and gas that absorbed the light of forming stars glow as they give it out again. That glow traces a network of cavernous bubbles and filament-like shells, carved by young stars pouring energy into the spiral arms. Webb also picks out several very bright star clusters near the core, and newly found young clusters along the outer edges of the bar where it joins the arms, which only Webb can see through the thick dust there.

NGC 1365 is one of the largest galaxies known, twice the length of the Milky Way. It is one of 19 galaxies studied by the PHANGS collaboration, which aims to learn how the birth of young stars affects the evolution of their galaxies.

understand.summary: Webb's MIRI took this mid-infrared image. NASA shows F770W in blue, F1000W and F1130W in green, and F2100W in red.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the eye. The PHANGS team says areas that are completely dark in Hubble images of these galaxies light up in detail in Webb's infrared views.

explore: The images also show how the orbits of stars and gas depend on where they form, which accounts for the older clusters found outside the galaxy's inner ring of star formation. The PHANGS team has also observed its galaxies with Hubble, the Very Large Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array. MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA.
